title: Functions
description: Questions on functions and their graphs, polynomials, exponentials and logarithms.

questions.question: Which of these rules is a function on all numbers?
questions.explanation: A function gives every input in its domain exactly one output (:ref{#function}). Two square roots is two outputs, and $$\frac{1}{x}$$ and $$\sqrt{x}$$ have no output at some numbers.

questions.question: What is the domain of the formula $$\frac{1}{x^2 - 9}$$?
questions.explanation: With no domain named, the domain is every $$x$$ where the formula makes sense (:ref{#formula-domain}). Here that means $$x^2 \ne 9$$.

questions.question: What is the range of $$x \mapsto x^2 + 1$$ on all numbers?
questions.explanation: Squares are never negative, so every value is at least $$1$$, and $$y \ge 1$$ is reached at $$x = \sqrt{y - 1}$$ (:ref{#range}).

questions.question: Are $$x \mapsto \frac{x^2}{x}$$ and $$x \mapsto x$$ the same function?
options: No: the first isn't defined at $$0$$
questions.explanation: Equal functions need the same domain as well as the same values (:ref{#function-equality}). They agree everywhere except $$0$$, where the first has no value.

questions.question: Let $$f(x) = x - 1$$ and $$g(x) = x^2$$. What is $$(g \circ f)(3)$$?
questions.explanation: $$g \circ f$$ means $$f$$ first, then $$g$$ (:ref{#function-composite}): $$f(3) = 2$$, then $$g(2) = 4$$. Doing $$g$$ first gives $$8$$.

questions.question: What is the inverse of $$f(x) = 3x - 5$$?
questions.explanation: Solve $$y = 3x - 5$$ for $$x$$ (:ref{#inverse-function}). Check: $$f(4) = 7$$ and $$\frac{7 + 5}{3} = 4$$. And $$f^{-1}$$ is not $$\frac{1}{f}$$.

questions.question: Why doesn't squaring on all numbers have an inverse?
options: It isn't one to one: $$3$$ and $$-3$$ both give $$9$$
questions.explanation: An inverse needs one input for each value (:ref{#one-to-one}). On $$x \ge 0$$ squaring is one to one, and $$\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$$ undoes it.

questions.question: The point $$(2, 5)$$ is on the graph of $$f$$. What does that say?
questions.explanation: The graph is the points $$(x, f(x))$$ (:ref{#function-graph}): go up from $$2$$ and across to $$5$$.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT the graph of a function?
options: The top half of a circle
questions.explanation: The vertical line $$x = 0$$ meets the circle at $$(0, 3)$$ and $$(0, -3)$$, so it fails the vertical line test (:ref{#vertical-line-test}).

questions.question: What is $$\lfloor -2.5 \rfloor$$?
questions.explanation: The floor is the largest integer $$\le x$$ (:ref{#floor}). $$-2$$ is bigger than $$-2.5$$, so the floor is $$-3$$.

questions.question: Where is $$(x + 2)(x - 3)$$ negative?
questions.explanation: Between the roots one factor is positive and the other negative, so the product is negative (:ref{#real-numbers/product-sign}). Outside the roots the factors have the same sign.

questions.question: Why is an increasing function one to one?
options: Different inputs give one smaller and one larger value
questions.explanation: If $$x < y$$ then $$f(x) < f(y)$$, so the values differ (:ref{#graphs-increasing-one-to-one}).

questions.question: How does the graph of $$y = \lvert x - 4 \rvert$$ sit compared with $$y = \lvert x \rvert$$?
questions.explanation: $$f(x - h)$$ slides the graph by $$h$$ to the right (:ref{#function-graph-moves}). The new graph at $$x$$ does what the old one did at $$x - 4$$.

questions.question: How is the graph of $$y = 3f(x)$$ moved from the graph of $$f$$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the output stretches upwards (:ref{#function-graph-moves}). Changing the input, as in $$f(3x)$$, squeezes across instead.

questions.question: Which function is odd?
questions.explanation: $$(-x)^3 - (-x) = -(x^3 - x)$$, so $$f(-x) = -f(x)$$ (:ref{#even-odd-function}). The second and third are even, and the last is neither.

questions.question: What symmetry does the graph of an odd function have?
questions.explanation: $$f(-x) = -f(x)$$ says $$(x, y)$$ on the graph gives $$(-x, -y)$$ on the graph (:ref{#even-odd-graphs}).

questions.question: If $$f$$ is odd and $$g$$ is odd, what is $$fg$$?
questions.explanation: $$f(-x)g(-x) = (-f(x))(-g(x)) = f(x)g(x)$$, like two minus signs (:ref{#even-odd-arithmetic}). For example $$x \cdot x^3 = x^4$$.

questions.question: What is the even part of $$f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 - x + 4$$?
questions.explanation: The even part is $$\frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2}$$ (:ref{#even-odd-parts}). For a polynomial it collects the even powers.

questions.question: How is the graph of $$f^{-1}$$ related to the graph of $$f$$?
options: It is the mirror image in the $$x$$-axis
It is the half turn about $$O$$
It is the mirror image in the line $$y = x$$
questions.explanation: $$(a, b)$$ is on the graph of $$f$$ exactly when $$(b, a)$$ is on the graph of $$f^{-1}$$, and the flip in $$y = x$$ swaps the coordinates (:ref{#inverse-graph}).

questions.question: What is the degree of $$(2x^3 - x + 1)(x^2 + 5)$$?
questions.explanation: Degrees add when you multiply (:ref{#degree-product}): $$3 + 2 = 5$$. The leading coefficient is $$2 \cdot 1 = 2$$.

questions.question: $$1$$, $$2$$ and $$3$$ are roots of $$x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6$$. What is its factored form?
questions.explanation: With $$n$$ different roots, $$f(x) = a_n(x - c_1)\cdots(x - c_n)$$ (:ref{#factor-by-roots}), and here $$a_n = 1$$.

questions.question: At most how many roots can a polynomial of degree $$5$$ have?
questions.explanation: A polynomial of degree $$n$$ has at most $$n$$ roots (:ref{#root-bound}). Each root splits off a factor $$x - c$$ (:ref{#factor-theorem}).

questions.question: Why does the degree of a polynomial make sense?
options: Two formulas for the same function have the same coefficients
questions.explanation: If two formulas agreed everywhere, their difference would have infinitely many roots, so its coefficients are all $$0$$ (:ref{#coefficients-unique}).

questions.question: Which numbers can be whole-number roots of $$x^3 + 2x^2 - 5x - 6$$?
questions.explanation: With integer coefficients and leading coefficient $$1$$, an integer root divides the constant term (:ref{#integer-root}). Trying them, $$-1$$, $$2$$ and $$-3$$ work.

questions.question: What are the real roots of $$x^4 - 1$$?
questions.explanation: For even $$n$$, $$x^n = 1$$ has the two real solutions $$\pm 1$$ (:ref{#power-plus-minus-one}).

questions.question: A polynomial $$f$$ has $$f(2) = 0$$. Is $$f$$ the zero polynomial?
options: Not necessarily: it only has $$2$$ as a root
questions.explanation: The zero polynomial is $$0$$ at every number, with every coefficient $$0$$ (:ref{#degree}). Being $$0$$ at one number makes $$2$$ a root (:ref{#polynomial-root}).

questions.question: What is the remainder when $$x^4 - 3x + 1$$ is divided by $$x - 2$$?
questions.explanation: The remainder on dividing by $$x - c$$ is $$f(c)$$ (:ref{#remainder-theorem}): $$16 - 6 + 1 = 11$$.

questions.question: What is the remainder when $$x^3 - 2x^2 + 5$$ is divided by $$x + 1$$?
questions.explanation: $$x + 1 = x - (-1)$$, so the remainder is $$f(-1) = -1 - 2 + 5 = 2$$ (:ref{#remainder-theorem}).

questions.question: Dividing a polynomial by $$x^2 + 1$$, what can the remainder be?
options: $$0$$ or a polynomial of degree at most $$1$$
questions.explanation: The remainder is $$0$$ or has smaller degree than what you divide by (:ref{#polynomial-division}), like a remainder smaller than the divisor for whole numbers.

questions.question: What is the domain of $$\frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$$?
questions.explanation: A rational function is defined where its denominator isn't $$0$$ (:ref{#rational-function}). It equals $$x + 1$$ except at $$1$$, where it has no value.

questions.question: When does $$x - c$$ divide a polynomial $$f$$?
options: Exactly when $$c$$ divides the constant term
questions.explanation: The remainder is $$f(c)$$, so it is $$0$$ exactly when $$c$$ is a root (:ref{#remainder-theorem}).

questions.question: How is $$2^{\sqrt 2}$$ given a meaning?
questions.explanation: Fractional powers closing in on $$\sqrt 2$$ give numbers closing in on about $$2.665$$. The rules for $$a^x$$ are then taken as given (:ref{#exponential-rules}).

questions.question: What is $$2^{-3}$$?
questions.explanation: $$a^{-x} = \frac{1}{a^x}$$ (:ref{#exponential-positive}). A negative exponent never gives a negative number.

questions.question: Can $$a^x$$ ever be $$0$$ or negative, for $$a > 0$$?
questions.explanation: Every exponential is positive (:ref{#exponential-positive}). That's why $$2^x = -1$$ has no solution.

questions.question: How does the graph of $$\left(\frac12\right)^x$$ relate to the graph of $$2^x$$?
options: It is its mirror image in the $$x$$-axis
It is its mirror image in the $$y$$-axis
questions.explanation: $$\left(\frac12\right)^x = 2^{-x}$$, and $$f(-x)$$ flips in the $$y$$-axis (:ref{#exponential-small-base}).

questions.question: $$500$$ bacteria double every $$20$$ minutes. How many after an hour?
questions.explanation: An hour is three doublings: $$500 \cdot 2^3 = 4000$$. Equal steps multiply by equal factors (:ref{#exponential-steps}).

questions.question: A medicine has a half-life of $$6$$ hours. Of an $$80$$ mg dose, how much is left after $$12$$ hours?
questions.explanation: Two half-lives: $$80 \to 40 \to 20$$. Decay never reaches $$0$$ (:ref{#growth-decay}).

questions.question: Which sign tells you a quantity changes exponentially?
options: Equal time steps multiply it by the same factor
Equal time steps add the same amount
questions.explanation: $$f(t + s) = f(t) \cdot a^{ks}$$, the same factor whatever $$t$$ is (:ref{#exponential-steps}). Adding the same amount is linear change.

questions.question: What is $$\log_2 32$$?
questions.explanation: $$2^5 = 32$$, and $$\log_a y$$ is the power that gives $$y$$ (:ref{#logarithm}).

questions.question: What is $$\log_3 \frac{1}{9}$$?
questions.explanation: $$3^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}$$ (:ref{#logarithm}). Logarithms of numbers between $$0$$ and $$1$$ are negative when the base is above $$1$$.

questions.question: What is $$\log_4 2$$?
questions.explanation: $$4^{1/2} = \sqrt 4 = 2$$, so the power is $$\frac12$$ (:ref{#logarithm}).

questions.question: What is $$\log_a(xy)$$?
questions.explanation: Multiplying adds the counts of factors of $$a$$ (:ref{#log-laws}): $$\log_2(8 \cdot 4) = 3 + 2 = 5$$.

questions.question: What is $$\log_2(8 + 8)$$?
questions.explanation: $$8 + 8 = 16 = 2^4$$. There is no law for the logarithm of a sum, so $$\log_2 8 + \log_2 8 = 6$$ is the wrong answer (:ref{#log-laws}).

questions.question: Which of these equals $$\log_{10}(x^2)$$ for $$x > 0$$?
questions.explanation: The power law: $$\log_a(x^r) = r\log_a x$$ (:ref{#log-laws}). At $$x = 1000$$: $$\log_{10} 1000^2 = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$$, while $$(\log_{10} 1000)^2 = 9$$.

questions.question: How do you find $$\log_2 10$$ with a calculator that has only $$\log_{10}$$?
questions.explanation: Change of base: $$\log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b}$$ (:ref{#change-of-base}). Check: $$2^{3.32} \approx 10$$.

questions.question: Through which point does the graph of every $$\log_a$$ pass?
questions.explanation: $$\log_a 1 = 0$$ since $$a^0 = 1$$. The graph is the graph of $$a^x$$, which passes through $$(0, 1)$$, flipped in $$y = x$$ (:ref{#log-graph}).

questions.question: Solve $$3 \cdot 2^x = 48$$.
questions.explanation: Divide by $$3$$: $$2^x = 16$$, so $$x = \log_2 16 = 4$$ (:ref{#log-inverse}).

questions.question: For which numbers $$x$$ is $$\log_{10} x$$ defined?
questions.explanation: $$\log_a$$ undoes $$a^x$$, whose values are the positive numbers, so its domain is the positive numbers (:ref{#log-inverse}).

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: £1 earns $$100\%$$ a year, paid in $$12$$ monthly parts. About how much is there after a year?
questions.explanation: $$\left(1 + \frac{1}{12}\right)^{12} \approx 2.613$$. Paying more often gets closer to $$e \approx 2.718$$ but never past it (:ref{#e-exists}).

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: What is $$\ln e^3$$?
questions.explanation: $$\ln = \log_e$$ undoes $$e^x$$ (:ref{#natural-log}, :ref{#log-inverse}).

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: How can $$2^t$$ be written as a power of $$e$$?
questions.explanation: $$a^x = e^{x\ln a}$$ (:ref{#base-e}), since $$e^{\ln 2} = 2$$.

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: A population grows like $$Ce^{0.1t}$$, with $$t$$ in years. About how long does it take to double?
questions.explanation: The doubling time is $$\frac{\ln 2}{K} = \frac{0.693}{0.1}$$ (:ref{#half-life}), whatever the starting amount.

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: Why doesn't the starting amount $$C$$ matter when finding the rate $$K$$ from two measurements?
options: Dividing one measurement by the other cancels it
questions.explanation: $$\frac{f(t_2)}{f(t_1)} = \frac{Ce^{Kt_2}}{Ce^{Kt_1}} = e^{K(t_2 - t_1)}$$ (:ref{#rate-from-two}).

questions.topic: The number e and using logarithms
questions.question: Savings grow by $$5\%$$ a year. About how long until they double?
questions.explanation: Solve $$1.05^t = 2$$: $$t = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.05} \approx 14.2$$ (:ref{#log-laws}).
